subject: How to get estimates for area with no observation in spatial models, like BYM2

messages.author: 80b903b54c9cf4bd
messages.subject: How to get estimates for area with no observation in spatial models, like BYM2
parts:
Hi, 
Consider the situation in small area estimation where I have, say, 100 areas but only 60 of them have responses from a survey. Is that possible to build a spatial model to get the estimated responses for area with no observation? To be specific, let y_i is the number of people smoking in area i, then my model would looks like:
y_i ~ Binomial(p_i, m_i)//where m_i is the population
logit(p_i) = intercept + X*beta + b

where X is covariate, beta is fixed effect, and b is random effect following either Besag model, BYM,  BYM2, or BYM2 model. 

I have already got some result from when assuming b ~ CAR(rho, C) which is the proper CAR model. Although for some b_i s there is no observation, but the structure of the CAR model can help me get the estimates. I wonder how can use the spatial models like BYM2 to achieve the same purpose?

I noticed that for RW1 and RW2 models, we can have a parameter called values to indicate we want the estimates at those values. But there is no option for spatial structured models. I guess I can have an alternative way to work it out? 

Thanks,
Jiang

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to get estimates for area with no observation in spatial models, like BYM2

You do it with NAs.  See here: http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-How-can-I-do-predictions-using-INLA-

messages.author: 80b903b54c9cf4bd
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to get estimates for area with no observation in spatial models, like BYM2
parts:
Hi,
I'm playing with the NA values to make sure I can have the correct result before going to my own model. Here I attached the testing code I'm playing with.
The Model:
y_i ~ Binomial(p_i, Ntrials_i)
logit(p_i) = a + b*x

where i=1,...,100 for 100 observations. 

I have 5 locations to predict, with y_pred set to NAs, and Ntrials_pred is known number of trials. The covariates z_pred is also known.

The goal:
In a Bayesian setting, y_pred_i will be a random variable, thus the sum_y = y_pred_1+...+y_pred_5 should also be a random variable having some posterior predictive distribution. The following proportion is what I want:
proportion = sum_y/(Ntrials_1 + ... + Ntrials_5)

How I did in MCMC:
When I have posterior samples of logit(p_i), at each iteration, y_pred_i is got from rbinom(p_i, Ntrials_i), then sum_y is calculated at this iteration, so does the proportion I want. With many iterations, I have the posterior sample for the proportion, thus I got the mean as the estimate.

How should I do with inla?
1. Is there a way to calculate the marginal distribution of the proportion directly?
2. If 1 is not possible, then we need to use simulations. 
   2.1. Each p_i can be simulated, so does y_pred_i and the sum. However, I think it is wrong to do that by sampling them separately. Like in a MCMC settings, those posterior samples may be correlated. I am not sure if the result will be the same.
   2.2. Can I sample the proportion directly? How to do it correctly?

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to get estimates for area with no observation in spatial models, like BYM2
parts:
For data level predictions, you can use inla.posterior.sample() to sample from the joint posterior of the predictor, and then sample y-values conditionally on that. This does take the appropriate dependencies into account.

Finn

r = inla(formula, family = "binomial", data = data, Ntrials=c(Ntrials, Ntrials_pred),control.predictor = list(link = 1),
         control.compute = list(config=TRUE))
n_sim = 30000
xx = inla.posterior.sample(n_sim, r)
names_pred = paste('Predictor:', 101:105, sep='')
proportion_sample = numeric(n_sim)
for(i in 1:n_sim){
  eta_sample_i = as.numeric(xx[[i]]$latent[names_pred,])
  p_sample_i = exp(eta_sample_i)/(1+exp(eta_sample_i))
  proportion_sample[i] = sum(p_sample_i * Ntrials_pred)/sum(Ntrials_pred)
}
plot(density(proportion_sample))
mean(proportion_sample)

On 29 Sep 2017, at 07:56, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

For data level predictions, you can use inla.posterior.sample() to sample from the joint posterior of the predictor, and then sample y-values conditionally on that. This does take the appropriate dependencies into account.

Finn

On 29 Sep 2017, at 07:44, Jiang Du <jiang...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi,
I'm playing with the NA values to make sure I can have the correct result before going to my own model. Here I attached the testing code I'm playing with.
The Model:
y_i ~ Binomial(p_i, Ntrials_i)
logit(p_i) = a + b*x

where i=1,...,100 for 100 observations. 

I have 5 locations to predict, with y_pred set to NAs, and Ntrials_pred is known number of trials. The covariates z_pred is also known.

The goal:
In a Bayesian setting, y_pred_i will be a random variable, thus the sum_y = y_pred_1+...+y_pred_5 should also be a random variable having some posterior predictive distribution. The following proportion is what I want:
proportion = sum_y/(Ntrials_1 + ... + Ntrials_5)

How I did in MCMC:
When I have posterior samples of logit(p_i), at each iteration, y_pred_i is got from rbinom(p_i, Ntrials_i), then sum_y is calculated at this iteration, so does the proportion I want. With many iterations, I have the posterior sample for the proportion, thus I got the mean as the estimate.

How should I do with inla?
1. Is there a way to calculate the marginal distribution of the proportion directly?
2. If 1 is not possible, then we need to use simulations. 
   2.1. Each p_i can be simulated, so does y_pred_i and the sum. However, I think it is wrong to do that by sampling them separately. Like in a MCMC settings, those posterior samples may be correlated. I am not sure if the result will be the same.
   2.2. Can I sample the proportion directly? How to do it correctly?

On 28 September 2017 at 17:50, Jiang Du <jiang...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi, 
Consider the situation in small area estimation where I have, say, 100 areas but only 60 of them have responses from a survey. Is that possible to build a spatial model to get the estimated responses for area with no observation? To be specific, let y_i is the number of people smoking in area i, then my model would looks like:
y_i ~ Binomial(p_i, m_i)//where m_i is the population
logit(p_i) = intercept + X*beta + b

where X is covariate, beta is fixed effect, and b is random effect following either Besag model, BYM,  BYM2, or BYM2 model. 

I have already got some result from when assuming b ~ CAR(rho, C) which is the proper CAR model. Although for some b_i s there is no observation, but the structure of the CAR model can help me get the estimates. I wonder how can use the spatial models like BYM2 to achieve the same purpose?

I noticed that for RW1 and RW2 models, we can have a parameter called values to indicate we want the estimates at those values. But there is no option for spatial structured models. I guess I can have an alternative way to work it out? 

Thanks,
Jiang
